title: Safety, ESD and the technician's toolkit
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: Learn how to protect both yourself and the hardware: control static electricity, work safely around electricity, dispose of components responsibly, and build the toolkit every helpdesk technician carries.
objectives: Explain what electrostatic discharge is and why tiny static charges destroy components
Apply ESD prevention using an anti-static wrist strap, ESD mat, and anti-static bags
Identify electrical hazards and explain why a PSU and CRT monitor must never be opened
Apply personal and environmental safety practices for lifting, fire, fumes, and cables
Explain how to dispose of batteries, toner, and e-waste safely using SDS sheets
Identify the core tools in a technician's toolkit and what each one is for

quiz.q: Why can a static shock you cannot even feel still destroy a computer component?
options: Components are too cheap to survive any handling
Sensitive chips can be damaged by far less voltage than a human can feel
Static only damages the case, never the chips
Modern parts are immune to static
quiz.why: You typically only feel static above about three thousand volts, but sensitive electronics can be damaged by under a hundred volts, so harmful ESD happens invisibly.

quiz.q: Why should you never open a power supply unit or a CRT monitor?
options: The screws are glued in permanently
They contain capacitors that hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged
They are too heavy to open safely
quiz.why: PSUs and CRTs hold large capacitors that can store a lethal charge for a long time after being unplugged, so they are non-serviceable for a helpdesk technician.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store a spare RAM stick or expansion card?
options: Taped to the side of the tower
quiz.why: Anti-static bags are designed to safely shield components from static build-up; pockets, wool, and carpets all generate static that can damage parts.

quiz.q: Which practice reduces ESD risk while you work inside a PC?
options: Working on a thick carpet in socks
Wearing an anti-static wrist strap clipped to the chassis
Rubbing the parts to remove dust
quiz.why: An anti-static wrist strap bonds you to the same electrical potential as the chassis (equipotential bonding) so charge cannot build up and jump to a component.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does an SDS (Safety Data Sheet) tell a technician?
quiz.answer: An SDS explains the hazards of a material such as toner or a battery and how to handle, store, and dispose of it safely.
quiz.why: SDS sheets (formerly called MSDS) are the standard reference for handling and disposal of potentially hazardous materials in the workplace.

quiz.q: Name two tools you would expect in a basic technician's toolkit and say what each is for.
quiz.answer: Examples: a screwdriver set for removing case and component screws, an anti-static wrist strap to prevent ESD, a spudger for prying clips without scratching, a flashlight to see inside the case, or compressed air to clear dust.
quiz.why: A helpdesk toolkit mixes mechanical tools (screwdrivers, spudger), safety gear (wrist strap), and diagnostic tools (multimeter, cable tester) plus cleaning supplies.

body_markdown:
## What is ESD and why does it matter

**Electrostatic discharge (ESD)** is the sudden flow of electricity between two objects at different charges — the tiny zap you feel touching a door handle. You only *feel* static above about **3,000 volts**, but sensitive chips inside a PC can be damaged by **less than 100 volts**. That means you can quietly destroy a part — or weaken it so it fails weeks later — without ever feeling a thing. This is why ESD is the number one hazard to the *hardware* you touch.

## Preventing ESD

The goal is to keep you and the equipment at the **same electrical potential** so no charge can jump. This is called **equipotential bonding**.

```text
ESD prevention checklist
[ ] Wear an anti-static wrist strap, clipped to bare metal on the chassis
[ ] Work on an ESD (anti-static) mat, not a carpet
[ ] Touch the metal case before handling any component
[ ] Hold cards by the edges, never the gold contacts or chips
[ ] Keep spare parts inside anti-static bags until needed
[ ] Avoid wool jumpers and shuffling on carpet in socks
```

An **anti-static wrist strap** connects your skin to the chassis through a resistor. An **ESD mat** does the same for your work surface. Together they drain static harmlessly instead of letting it build up and discharge into a chip.

## Electrical safety

Protect yourself, not just the parts. **Always power down properly and unplug the device before opening it.** Two components must **never** be opened by a helpdesk technician: the **power supply unit (PSU)** and a **CRT monitor**. Both contain large **capacitors** that store a dangerous — potentially lethal — charge for a long time *even after being unplugged*. These are non-serviceable: if one fails, you replace the whole unit.

## Personal and environmental safety

- **Lifting:** bend at the knees, keep your back straight, and get help with heavy servers or monitors.
- **Fire:** for electrical fires use a **CO2 extinguisher** (or another rated for electrical fires) — never water.
- **Fumes:** work in a ventilated space; some cleaning chemicals and overheated parts give off harmful fumes.
- **Trip hazards:** keep cables tidy and routed away from walkways. Good **cable management** is a safety measure, not just neatness.

## Proper disposal

Many IT items are hazardous waste and must **never** go in normal bins:

- **Batteries** (including the small CMOS coin cell) — recycle at proper collection points.
- **Toner and ink** — return cartridges through recycling schemes; toner powder is harmful to breathe.
- **E-waste** (old PCs, monitors, cables) — use a certified electronics recycler.

When in doubt, check the **SDS (Safety Data Sheet)**, formerly called an **MSDS**. It lists a material's hazards and how to handle, store, and dispose of it safely.

## The technician's toolkit

A good kit mixes mechanical, safety, and diagnostic tools:

- **Screwdriver set** (Phillips/flat, magnetic tip) — open cases and fasten components.
- **Spudger** — safely pry plastic clips without scratching boards.
- **Anti-static wrist strap** — your ESD protection.
- **Multimeter** — check voltages and continuity.
- **Cable tester** — confirm network cables are wired correctly.
- **Flashlight** — see inside dark cases.
- **Compressed air** — blow dust out of fans and heatsinks.
- **Thermal paste** — reapply between a CPU and its cooler.

## Your task

Write your own ESD and safety checklist (you can copy the one above and add to it). Then look around your own desk: identify at least three trip hazards or cable-management problems and note how you would fix each. Finally, list which everyday IT items in your home — old batteries, a dead phone, an ink cartridge — should be recycled as e-waste rather than thrown in the bin.

slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson Nine. Before you ever open a computer, you need to know how to keep both yourself and the hardware safe. In this lesson we'll cover E S D, electrical safety, personal and environmental safety, proper disposal, and the toolkit every helpdesk technician carries.

slides.title: What is ESD?
bullets: ESD is a sudden flow of static between objects.
It's the zap you feel on a door handle.
You only feel it above about three thousand volts.
Chips can be harmed by under a hundred volts.
slides.narration: Let's start with the biggest threat to the hardware: electrostatic discharge, or E S D. It's that little zap you feel when you touch a door handle. Here's the catch. You only feel static above about three thousand volts, but the sensitive chips inside a P C can be damaged by less than a hundred volts. So you can destroy a part without feeling a thing.

slides.title: Why tiny static is deadly to parts
bullets: Damage can be invisible and instant.
Or it can weaken a part so it fails later.
Carpet and wool jumpers build up charge.
Keep yourself and the PC at the same potential.
slides.narration: Because the damage is invisible, E S D is sneaky. Sometimes a part dies instantly; other times it's weakened and fails weeks later, which is much harder to diagnose. Shuffling on carpet or wearing a wool jumper builds up charge on your body. The whole goal is to keep you and the computer at the same electrical potential so nothing jumps across.

slides.title: Preventing ESD
bullets: Wear an anti-static wrist strap on the chassis.
Use an ESD mat, never work on carpet.
Store spare parts in anti-static bags.
Hold cards by the edges, not the contacts.
slides.code:
ESD prevention checklist
[ ] Wrist strap clipped to bare metal
[ ] Work on an ESD mat
[ ] Touch the metal case first

slides.narration: Prevention is simple and cheap. Wear an anti-static wrist strap clipped to bare metal on the chassis. Work on an E S D mat, never on carpet. Always touch the metal case before you handle a component, hold cards by their edges, and keep any spare parts inside anti-static bags until the moment you need them.

slides.title: Equipotential bonding
bullets: The wrist strap links your skin to the chassis.
Through a resistor, so charge drains safely.
You and the PC sit at the same potential.
No difference means no damaging discharge.
slides.narration: The technical name for this is equipotential bonding, but the idea is easy. The wrist strap connects your skin to the chassis through a resistor, so any static on you drains away gently instead of zapping a chip. When you and the P C are at the same potential, there's no difference for electricity to jump across, and your components stay safe.

slides.title: Electrical safety
bullets: Always power down and unplug before opening.
Never open a PSU or a CRT monitor.
Their capacitors hold a dangerous charge.
That charge stays even after unplugging.
slides.narration: Now safety for you. Always shut the device down properly and unplug it before you open it. And here's a rule with no exceptions: never open a P S U, the power supply unit, or a C R T monitor. Both hold large capacitors that store a dangerous, even lethal charge long after they're unplugged. They are non-serviceable, so you replace the whole unit.

slides.title: Personal & environmental safety
bullets: Lift with your knees, not your back.
Use a CO2 extinguisher on electrical fires.
Ventilate to avoid harmful fumes.
Tidy cables to remove trip hazards.
slides.narration: Look after your body and your workspace too. Lift heavy gear with your knees, not your back, and get help with servers and monitors. For an electrical fire, use a C O 2 extinguisher, never water. Work somewhere ventilated, and keep cables tidy and out of walkways. Good cable management isn't just neatness, it stops people tripping.

slides.title: Proper disposal
bullets: Batteries, including the CMOS coin cell, get recycled.
Toner and ink cartridges go to recycling schemes.
E-waste goes to a certified recycler.
Check the SDS sheet for handling and disposal.
slides.narration: A lot of IT gear is hazardous waste and must never go in a normal bin. Batteries, including the little C MOS coin cell, get recycled at proper points. Toner and ink cartridges go through recycling schemes. Old PCs and monitors are e-waste for a certified recycler. When you're unsure how to handle something, check its S D S sheet, the safety data sheet.

slides.title: The technician's toolkit
bullets: Screwdrivers, spudger, anti-static wrist strap.
Multimeter and cable tester for diagnostics.
Flashlight and compressed air.
Thermal paste for the CPU cooler.
slides.code:
Core kit:
- Screwdriver set (magnetic)
- Spudger
- Anti-static wrist strap
- Multimeter + cable tester
- Flashlight + compressed air
- Thermal paste
slides.narration: Finally, your toolkit. You'll want a magnetic screwdriver set, a spudger for prying plastic clips without scratching, and your anti-static wrist strap. For diagnostics, a multimeter checks voltages and a cable tester confirms network wiring. Add a flashlight, compressed air for dust, and thermal paste for when you reseat a C P U cooler.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: ESD destroys parts you can't feel — strap and mat.
Never open a PSU or CRT; they hold charge.
Recycle batteries, toner, and e-waste; check the SDS.
Know your core toolkit and what each tool does.
Task: write a safety checklist and spot your hazards.
slides.narration: Let's recap. E S D can destroy parts with charges you'll never feel, so use a wrist strap and an E S D mat. Never open a P S U or a C R T monitor, because their capacitors hold a dangerous charge. Recycle batteries, toner, and e-waste, and check the S D S sheet when unsure. And know your toolkit. Your task: write your own E S D and safety checklist, find three trip or cable hazards at your desk and how you'd fix them, and list the home IT items that should be recycled as e-waste.
